headline: Yes
question: Gross price per MHz-pop in the FCC's upper C-band auction (Auction 115, 160 MHz at 3.98-4.14 GHz; bidding set to start 27 April 2027): gross bids divided by (MHz offered x 335M US pops). Resolves on the final round; void if bidding has not concluded by end-2028.
rationale: Our central estimate is $0.77 per MHz-pop, about $41B of bids for 160 MHz. That is below the lower C-band's own $0.87 on the same 335M-pop basis and close to the 3.45 GHz auction's $0.70. Each of the three carriers already holds about 150 MHz or more of mid-band, winners owe about $16B of clearing and altimeter costs on top of their bids (about $0.30 per MHz-pop), and AT&T is stretched after paying $23B for EchoStar spectrum. A serious SpaceX bid is the main upside. The range is wide because US auctions have missed consensus in both directions.
drivers_up: SpaceX bids seriously as a fourth bidder; Verizon or AT&T fight for blocks next to their existing C-band to build a 440 MHz contiguous range; carriers bid defensively after SpaceX's spectrum moves; little other new mid-band arrives before 2030.
drivers_down: About $16B of add-on costs; carrier debt (AT&T at 3.13x leverage, Verizon net debt $123.7B); Verizon's 4-5 year deployment lag; T-Mobile will only buy if cheaper than adding sites; the 2.7 GHz band follows in 2028; second tranches abroad cleared far lower (Canada 3800 MHz about 90% below 3500 MHz).
base_rate: US mid-band auctions in 2021-22 cleared $0.70-0.87 per MHz-pop on 335M pops; the 2015 AWS-3 peak was about $2.70. Analyst ranges (TD Cowen $30-75B, Carr $30-60B) imply $0.56-1.40. Five of the last eight big US auctions beat consensus, while 600 MHz and 2.5 GHz fell well short.
signposts: Auction 115 short-form filings (6-20 January 2027), especially whether SpaceX applies; the qualified-bidder list and upfront payments (around March 2027); bidding pace in the first weeks after the 27 April 2027 start.

question: Gross proceeds of the FCC upper C-band auction (Auction 115), in $B. Void if bidding has not concluded by end-2028.
rationale: Proceeds are the price forecast times 53.6B MHz-pops (160 MHz times 335M people), so about $41B at the middle. That sits inside Carr's $30-60B and TD Cowen's $30-75B ranges and far below the $81B raised for 280 MHz in 2021. If only the three carriers bid, and they hold back, proceeds land near $30B. If SpaceX bids hard, they land near $50B or more. The $72B top end allows for a surprise like the 2021 auction, which beat its forecast by 55-100%.
drivers_up: SpaceX or another new bidder; carriers paying up for blocks next to their C-band; a scarcity of other mid-band before 2030; strategic bidding to keep SpaceX out.
drivers_down: Only three committed bidders for eight blocks per market, which invites restraint; $16B of add-on costs; stretched balance sheets after the EchoStar deals; the FCC's refusal to give satellite coverage buildout credit, which deters SpaceX.
base_rate: Lower C-band ($81B) beat its $40-52B consensus. 3.45 GHz landed near consensus. 600 MHz (about half of forecasts) and 2.5 GHz (well below $1-5B estimates) fell short.
signposts: Whether SpaceX appears on the Auction 115 qualified-bidder list (early 2027); daily round results after 27 April 2027; gross bids passing $50.4B, the level that beats the 2021 price per MHz-pop.

headline: Yes
question: Median price per MHz-pop of US nationwide or near-nationwide low- and mid-band spectrum (below 6 GHz) changing hands in 2029-2030, across FCC auctions and private sales above $1B (nominal dollars).
rationale: We expect big 2029-30 deals to have a median near $0.90 per MHz-pop, below today's $1.40 AT&T-EchoStar benchmark. The likely deal set mixes cheap FCC auctions (2.7 GHz, 1675/2020 MHz, perhaps 4.4 or 7 GHz, at roughly $0.3-0.8) with dearer private sales of low-band and paired spectrum ($1.2-2.5). By 2030 mid-band supply is up about a third, which pushes generic mid-band down while low-band keeps its premium. With only a handful of qualifying deals, which deals happen decides the median, so the range is wide.
drivers_up: Private low-band or paired sales dominate the sample; SpaceX and Amazon keep buying; 2.7 GHz or 7 GHz auctions slip past 2030; traffic re-accelerates on AI uplink.
drivers_down: Several FCC auctions land in 2029-30 with federal exclusion zones and lots of MHz; carriers have room after upper C-band; SpaceX says its portfolio is complete; foreign mid-band prices keep falling.
base_rate: 2021-22 US auctions cleared $0.67-0.87 per MHz-pop; 2025-26 private sales ran $0.52-2.53 with a median near $1.20. Real US mid-band prices have fallen since 2015 as supply rose. Recent European mid-band averages are about $0.07.
signposts: The FCC's 2.7 GHz auction date and result (Carr targets 2028); the price of EchoStar's paired AWS-3 sale (promised by September 2028); any SpaceX or Amazon low-band purchase in 2028-30.

question: Number of US spectrum-only transactions of $5B or more announced from 1 Jan 2027 to 31 Dec 2030 (licence sales or swaps; FCC auctions excluded; company takeovers count only if spectrum is most of the value).
current_label: 3 spectrum-only deals in 2025-26 (AT&T and SpaceX from EchoStar; SpaceX from Grain), plus Amazon-Globalstar ($11.6B takeover)
rationale: We expect one spectrum-only deal of $5B or more in 2027-30, with roughly a one-in-three chance of none. The most likely is EchoStar's paired AWS-3 remainder, marked near $8B, which EchoStar has promised to sell by September 2028, though it could be split into smaller pieces. Further buying by SpaceX or Amazon, or a carrier sale or swap after Auction 115, could add one or two more. Before 2025 such deals came about once every five years; the 2025-26 burst came from one forced seller and one new buyer.
drivers_up: SpaceX or Amazon want more terrestrial spectrum; EchoStar sells its AWS-3 in one block; Anterix or Ligado assets get re-rated; post-auction swaps between carriers.
drivers_down: Few large nationwide holdings remain outside the big three; SpaceX called 800 MHz its last critical piece; FCC concentration review; auctions offer an alternative supply route; EchoStar may sell in pieces under $5B.
base_rate: About 0.2 qualifying deals a year in 2013-24; three in 2025-26 (AT&T and SpaceX from EchoStar, SpaceX from Grain).
signposts: An EchoStar paired AWS-3 sale announcement (deadline September 2028); SpaceX comments on spectrum needs after Grain closes (mid-2027); Amazon's terrestrial spectrum plans once Globalstar closes (2027).

headline: Yes
question: US wireless data traffic in calendar 2030 as reported by CTIA's annual survey (includes fixed wireless), in exabytes (trillion MB) per year.
rationale: We expect about 330 EB in 2030, roughly double 2025's 159 EB, with yearly growth fading from 20% to about 12% (about 15.5% a year on average). Bottom-up, phones at about 37 GB a month give about 150 EB, and about 28M fixed wireless lines at about 520 GB a month give about 175 EB. Mature markets show the same slowdown (UK +18%, Switzerland 20-25%), and 82-89% of phone data still rides Wi-Fi. The top of the range is CTIA's own 22%-a-year path, which industry forecasts have usually overshot.
drivers_up: Fixed wireless grows toward 30M+ lines on upper C-band capacity; multimodal AI and glasses add uplink; robotaxi fleets scale; video quality rises.
drivers_down: Fixed wireless adds keep slowing (Verizon 159K in Q3 2026 vs 261K); fiber overbuild by the same carriers; Wi-Fi offload; a saturated phone base; better video compression.
base_rate: Growth fell from 38% (2022) to 20% (2025). Ericsson forecasts 13% a year for North American smartphone data to 2031. Mature markets settle in the high teens or below.
signposts: Ericsson Mobility Report (30 November 2026 and June 2027); CTIA's survey of 2026 traffic (around September 2027); quarterly fixed wireless net adds from Verizon and AT&T.

question: US wireless data traffic in calendar 2035 on the CTIA basis, in exabytes per year.
rationale: We extend the 2030 path at about 10% a year, giving about 525 EB in 2035, roughly 3.3 times 2025. Every maturing market shows growth decaying, and Ericsson's own forecast slows to 14% by 2031. The range is wide and skewed up. The low end has growth near 6% after a weak 2030; the high end keeps growth near 16% on uplink-heavy AI devices, 6G and 7 GHz capacity.
drivers_up: Physical AI (robotaxis, drones, delivery robots) on wide-area networks; AI glasses and camera assistants; 7 GHz and 6G capacity making fixed wireless cheaper.
drivers_down: Fixed wireless shrinks under fiber overbuild; phone use plateaus; on-device AI cuts round trips; Wi-Fi 7 and 6 GHz unlicensed absorb more indoor traffic.
base_rate: Ericsson has repeatedly cut its forecasts (its 2030 global figure fell from 473 to 430 EB a month in one year). CTIA's 4x-by-2032 path (about 640 EB) sits above our 2032 range.
signposts: CTIA growth in 2027-28 (holding above 15% would lift this); US uplink share in Ookla and Opensignal data; robotaxi fleet counts (Waymo about 4,000 in September 2026).

headline: Yes
short: AI share of mobile traffic in 2030
question: Share of mobile network traffic directly attributable to AI assistants, agents and AI devices (glasses, robots, vehicles' AI functions) in 2030, on a narrow definition like Ericsson's 2025 GenAI measurement (not AI-recommended video), in percent. Resolves on the best operator or vendor measurement for 2030.
rationale: The only measurement is 0.06% of mobile traffic (Ericsson, April 2025). Reaching our 1.5% median by 2030 needs AI traffic to grow about 120% a year while total traffic grows 15-18%. Text AI is light, much inference runs on the device or server to server, and glasses and indoor robots mostly ride the phone or Wi-Fi. The upper tail is fat because camera and voice assistants and AI video apps could scale the way TikTok did, and the vendors who publish the measurement have reasons to count AI traffic broadly.
drivers_up: Always-on multimodal assistants; AI glasses (IDC sees 27M display-less units by 2030); AI video generation apps being counted; robotaxi uplink; generous vendor definitions.
drivers_down: On-device models; AI features folded into existing apps and not counted separately; Wi-Fi offload; robots on Wi-Fi or private 5G indoors.
base_rate: Broad-definition forecasts (GSMA 5-20% by 2030, Nokia 44% of all traffic by 2035) have a record of overshooting. Video took over a decade to reach about 75% of mobile traffic; TikTok reached double-digit share in about four years.
signposts: Any new operator or vendor AI traffic measurement (watch Ericsson's 30 November 2026 and June 2027 reports); AI glasses shipments in 2027; robotaxi fleet sizes and per-vehicle data use.

question: Combined fixed wireless access (home and business internet over the mobile network) subscribers of T-Mobile, Verizon and AT&T at end-2030, in millions.
rationale: We expect about 29M fixed wireless homes and businesses across the big three at end-2030, up from about 19M in Q3 2026. Net adds have already peaked (3.8M in 2025, about 3.6M in 2026), and we assume they keep decaying toward 2M a year. That lands close to the carriers' own targets: T-Mobile 15M by 2030, Verizon 'well beyond' 8-9M by 2028, AT&T about 5M. New Street's estimate of about 32M of Big 3 capacity caps the upside unless upper C-band adds room.
drivers_up: Upper C-band capacity from 2028-30; cable broadband price rises; AT&T's EchoStar 3.45 GHz enabling more Internet Air; steady T-Mobile adds.
drivers_down: Rising disconnects as the base grows; AT&T and Verizon pushing fiber first; carriers rationing capacity for mobile; satellite broadband competition; slower speeds at peak hours.
base_rate: Product S-curves flatten once 50-70% of capacity is used. Industry adds fell from 3.8M (2025) to about 3.6M (2026), and Verizon's Q3 2026 adds fell 39% year on year.
signposts: Quarterly fixed wireless net adds (Verizon and AT&T; T-Mobile stopped disclosing in 2026); any FWA price rises or sales pauses; the pace of upper C-band deployment after 2028.

question: US wireless service revenue divided by US wireless data traffic (CTIA basis) in 2030, in dollars per GB.
rationale: This is our revenue forecast ($266B) divided by our traffic forecast (328 EB), about $0.80 per GB in 2030 against $1.48 in 2025. That is a fall of about 11% a year, half the 2020-25 pace, because traffic growth is slowing while revenue still grows 2-3%. Traffic uncertainty drives nearly all of the range. Even our high case keeps falling every year, so this does not point to a capacity squeeze.
drivers_up: Slower traffic growth; carrier price rises; premium tiers for satellite, slicing or AI; carriers rationing cheap fixed wireless.
drivers_down: Faster traffic growth from fixed wireless and AI; cable free lines and SpaceX pricing; satellite service bundled free; flat revenue.
base_rate: Revenue per GB fell from $412 (2010) to $4.50 (2020) and $1.48 (2025), about -20% a year since 2020. CTIA reports price per MB fell 21% in 2025.
signposts: CTIA's annual revenue and traffic figures (each September); the BLS wireless price index after carrier price rises; any slowdown in fixed wireless selling.

headline: Yes
question: MHz of new licensed terrestrial mobile spectrum (not re-auctions of returned licences) for which FCC auction bidding concludes between 1 Jan 2026 and 31 Dec 2030.
current_label: None since 2022 (upper C-band 160 MHz scheduled for 2027)
rationale: Upper C-band (160 MHz) is close to certain and sets the floor. Our central case adds the 2.7 GHz band (about 210 MHz), which has approved federal relocation plans and a 2028 FCC target, for about 370 MHz. The 25 MHz 1675/2020 MHz band is roughly a coin flip. The top of the range needs a 7 GHz or 4.4 GHz auction to finish by 2030, which we put at about 30%, because US mid-band auctions usually slip 1-3 years from their first target.
drivers_up: Statutory deadline of 200 MHz of federal spectrum auctioned by July 2029; Carr's 2028 auction slate (2.7 GHz, 1.6 GHz, 7 GHz); NTIA claims to be ahead of schedule; fiscal need for auction revenue.
drivers_down: Defense Department resistance and relocation costs; FAA altimeter issues; NTIA study slips; litigation; once 300 MHz is auctioned, the law stops forcing more until 2033; political change after 2028.
base_rate: About 585 MHz was auctioned in 2015-22 (about 73 MHz a year), then none during the 2023-25 lapse in authority. US mid-band auctions have typically slipped 1-3 years.
signposts: NTIA's 7.125-7.4 GHz report (due 10 December 2026); FCC 2.7 GHz rules and auction date (2027-28); a final order on 1675/2020 MHz after the October 2026 proposal.

question: MHz of new licensed terrestrial mobile spectrum for which FCC auction bidding concludes between 1 Jan 2026 and 31 Dec 2035 (the 2025 law requires at least 300 MHz in 1.3-10.5 GHz by 2034 within an 800 MHz pipeline).
current_label: Law requires at least 300 MHz by 2034
rationale: The 2025 law sets an 800 MHz pipeline with at least 300 MHz auctioned by 2034, and our central case delivers about 640 MHz by 2035. That assumes upper C-band, 2.7 GHz and 7.125-7.4 GHz are done, plus part of 4.4-4.94 GHz about half the time. Statutory spectrum targets are usually met late or in part: about 75% of the 2012 Spectrum Act targets were auctioned within the decade. The law also excludes two big federal bands (3.1-3.45 and 7.4-8.4 GHz), and Defense Department resistance caps the upside.
drivers_up: WRC-27 identification of 7 GHz and 4.4 GHz for mobile; 6G demand; auction revenue needs; a possible mmWave auction that adds many MHz cheaply.
drivers_down: Defense Department preference for sharing over clearing; excluded bands; FCC auction authority lapsing in September 2034; weak bids reducing the fiscal push; shared and unlicensed alternatives.
base_rate: About 75% of Spectrum Act targets were met within a decade. The statutory minimum (300 MHz) is met by upper C-band plus 2.7 GHz alone.
signposts: WRC-27 decisions on 4.4-4.8 and 7.125-8.4 GHz (October-November 2027); NTIA's identification of the second federal tranche (due July 2029); progress on the nine 4.4 GHz relocation plans.

headline: Yes
question: MHz (nationwide-equivalent, both directions counted) of US spectrum usable for terrestrial or direct-to-device mobile service that SpaceX owns (closed transactions or auction wins, not leases from carriers) at end-2030.
current_label: 0 closed; about 79 MHz pending (EchoStar 65, Grain 14) plus small AWS-3 re-auction wins
rationale: SpaceX has about 79 MHz pending: 65 MHz from EchoStar (FCC-approved, closing targeted for 30 November 2027) and 14 MHz of 800 MHz from Grain (awaiting FCC approval). Our median of 88 MHz sits a little above that because at least one modest addition is slightly more likely than not: upper C-band wins (about 45%), EchoStar's paired AWS-3, the 2020-2025 MHz block next to its AWS-4, or 2.7 GHz. The floor near 66 MHz is the case where the Grain deal fails. Musk's description of 800 MHz as the 'last critical piece' keeps the median from going higher.
drivers_up: Meaningful upper C-band or 2.7 GHz wins; buying EchoStar's paired AWS-3; buying more low-band; SpaceX added about 79 MHz in 13 months.
drivers_down: FCC denial or tough conditions on Grain; an EchoStar closing failure; SpaceX capital going to AI; FCC refusal of satellite buildout credit, which makes auction licences costlier to hold.
base_rate: The FCC approved every major 2025-26 spectrum transfer, with conditions. SpaceX went from zero to about 79 MHz agreed in 13 months.
signposts: The FCC's Grain decision (petitions due 1 December 2026, decision likely mid-2027); SpaceX's Auction 115 short-form (January 2027) and winnings; the EchoStar closing on 30 November 2027.

question: Global direct-to-device (satellite to ordinary phones and IoT devices) service revenue in 2030, wholesale plus retail, all operators, in $B.
rationale: Satellite-to-phone revenue is well under $1B today, and we expect about $5B in 2030. Summing by operator: SpaceX wholesale from carrier partners plus any US retail (about $2-2.5B), AST's revenue share with its carrier partners (about $1B), and Apple/Amazon-Globalstar, China and IoT (about $1.5B combined). For scale, the whole legacy satellite-phone industry earns a few billion dollars a year, and carriers mostly bundle satellite service at near-zero extra price. The high end needs broadband-class next-generation service, due from 2027-28, to sell as a paid add-on.
drivers_up: Next-generation SpaceX satellites (about 20x per-satellite throughput) from 2027; Amazon entry around 2028; AST's ramp to 100+ satellites; car, IoT and wearable contracts; government deals.
drivers_down: Bundling at near-zero price; low willingness to pay outside emergencies; three or four constellations competing; Starship and launch slips.
base_rate: Iridium earned $0.87B in 2025; the whole legacy mobile-satellite industry earns a few billion a year. Forecasts for new satellite services have usually overshot.
signposts: Any SpaceX disclosure of Starlink Mobile revenue; AST reaching about 45 satellites (target mid-2027) and its 2027 revenue guidance; carrier pricing for satellite add-ons.

short: SpaceX's own US mobile subscribers in 2030
question: Paying US mobile subscribers billed directly by SpaceX/Starlink Mobile at end-2030 (excluding satellite add-ons billed by carrier partners), in millions.
rationale: We expect about 1M US subscribers billed directly by SpaceX at end-2030, with about a one-in-four chance of essentially none. SpaceX has said it plans its own US service once the EchoStar spectrum closes (targeted for 30 November 2027), and we put about 53% on a launch by end-2028. New entrants grow slowly: cable took about 8 years to reach 24M lines with tens of millions of broadband homes to sell to, and Dish/Boost never scaled on its own. The long upper tail covers a cheap plan bundled with Starlink broadband or buying an existing subscriber base.
drivers_up: An early-2028 launch; bundling with Starlink broadband homes; low prices; 800 MHz for indoor coverage; tower access deals; buying a regional carrier or a reseller base.
drivers_down: Satellites cannot serve dense indoor demand (over 70% of traffic is indoors); T-Mobile refuses an MVNO; phones need support for new bands; closing delays; SpaceX timelines that slip.
base_rate: Cable resellers reached about 1M lines in about 1.5 years and about 24M in about 8 years. Dish/Boost reached about 7M after 5 years, mostly through acquired customers.
signposts: A SpaceX consumer plan launch and its price (targeted for early 2028); tower access deals (SpaceX has sought about 80,000 sites); phones shipping in 2027-28 with AWS-4 and 800 MHz support.

headline: Yes
question: US wireless industry service revenue in 2030 on the CTIA basis, in nominal $B.
rationale: We expect about $266B in 2030, up about 2.5% a year from $235B in 2025. Industry revenue has grown about 3% a year in nominal terms since 2007, roughly flat after inflation, even as traffic rose by orders of magnitude. 2026 is firmer (AT&T wireless service +5%, T-Mobile +6-9%), and fixed wireless adds about 0.7 points a year. Cable's free lines, Verizon's falling ARPA and a possible SpaceX price war pull the other way.
drivers_up: Price rises in a three-network market; fixed wireless growth; T-Mobile-style ARPA gains (+4%); satellite and premium tiers; IoT lines.
drivers_down: Cable free lines (about half of Comcast connects); Verizon ARPA down 1.9%; SpaceX entry; a saturated phone base; falling price per GB.
base_rate: 2007-25 nominal growth was about 3% a year; Analysys Mason sees North American service revenue roughly flat to 2030. The $235B base comes from Light Reading citing CTIA; other trackers range $255-326B.
signposts: Verizon and T-Mobile ARPA trends each quarter; SpaceX's launch price (2028); CTIA's 2026 revenue figure (around September 2027).

question: Simple average EV/EBITDA (forward 12-month adjusted EBITDA) of AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile at end-2030.
rationale: We expect the big three to trade at about 6.9x forward EBITDA at end-2030, the same as today. US incumbent carriers have mostly traded between 6x and 8x, and today's level is close to that long-run average once T-Mobile's old premium is set aside. The market has punished each SpaceX spectrum step (carriers fell 9-13% on 9 October 2026), and an upper C-band and 6G spending cycle around 2030 weighs on cash flow. A takeover bid or rational three-network pricing could lift it above 8x.
drivers_up: Spectrum monetised through sales or M&A; a SpaceX or hyperscaler bid for a carrier; disciplined pricing among three networks; T-Mobile regaining some premium if SpaceX's build proves slow.
drivers_down: SpaceX entry and price pressure; cable share gains; a 2030 capex cycle; higher interest rates.
base_rate: US incumbent telcos have mostly traded at 6-8x. The research weights 2030 states at 50% grind (6-7.5x), 30% price pressure (5-6x) and 20% convergence premium (8x or more).
signposts: Carrier share moves on SpaceX milestones (Auction 115, 2028 launch); each carrier's upper C-band spend; T-Mobile's multiple versus AT&T and Verizon.

question: Combined Charter (including Cox) and Comcast mobile lines at end-2030, in millions.
rationale: Charter (including Cox) and Comcast had 24.1M mobile lines in Q3 2026 and added about 3.4M over the prior year. We assume adds decay about 10% a year, giving about 35M at end-2030; a straight-line trend gives about 38.6M. Shrinking cable broadband bases cap how many phone lines can be attached, and about half of Comcast's connects are free lines that may churn when promotions end. Cox's footprint inside Charter and the low-cost reseller model on Verizon's network keep growth going.
drivers_up: Free-line promotions; bundling to defend broadband; Cox integration; low mobile penetration of cable homes (about 20%); CBRS offload lowering costs.
drivers_down: Broadband losses (Comcast -144K and Charter -233K in Q3 2026); free-line roll-off; carrier retaliation on price; SpaceX as a new low-price rival.
base_rate: Cable added a steady 3-3.6M lines a year in 2022-26. Comcast's adds are already slowing (368K in Q3 2026 vs 414K a year earlier).
signposts: Quarterly cable mobile adds against the 876K Q3 2026 pace; cable broadband subscriber losses; any change to the Verizon wholesale terms.

question: US wireless industry network capital spending in 2030 on the CTIA basis, in nominal $B.
rationale: Industry network capex has been flat at $29-30B since 2023, after the 5G peak of $39B in 2022. We expect about $31.5B in 2030, as upper C-band deployment and early 6G start to lift spending from the trough, plus about 2.5% a year of inflation. Carriers are in harvest mode: Verizon trimmed its 2026 guide, AT&T cut its long-term outlook and T-Mobile guides about $10B. A return toward $39B needs a 2021-22-style spectrum-driven surge, which sits in our top tail.
drivers_up: Upper C-band builds (Verizon says 4-5 years); early 6G or 7 GHz overlays; densification for AI uplink; inflation.
drivers_down: Network sharing; capital shifting to fiber; vendor price competition; slowing traffic; heavy spending pushed to 2031-32.
base_rate: Past cycles peaked early in each generation then fell 20-30%; the 5G cycle rose 42% from 2018 to 2022, then fell 25% by 2024. 2030 sits near the turn from trough to ramp.
signposts: Carrier capex guidance for 2028-29 after Auction 115; the pace of upper C-band deployment; announced 6G build plans.
